qs.q: If $AB$ is defined where $A$ is symmetric and $B$ is not symmetric, then $AB$ ----
e: $AB$ is symmetric exactly when $(AB)^T=B^TA^T=AB$, which is not forced by the given information.
Example where it is symmetric: $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ (symmetric), $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ (not symmetric): $AB=0$ is symmetric.
Example where it is not symmetric: $A=I$, $B$ as above: $AB=B$ is not symmetric.
Both cases occur, so $AB$ may be symmetric.

qs.q: Suppose that $A_{3\times2}$ and $B_{2\times4}$ are two matrices. Then $AB$ ----
e: A symmetric matrix must satisfy $M=M^T$, which forces $M$ to be square (a $3\times4$ matrix has a $4\times3$ transpose).
Since $AB$ is not square, it can never be symmetric.
Transposing swaps rows and columns without changing entry values, so scalar multiples pass through: $(kA)^T=kA^T$.
With $k=2$: $(2A)^T=2A^T$. (The factor $4=2^2$ appears in $\det(2A)$, not in the transpose.)

e: $(A^T-A)^T=A-A^T=-(A^T-A)$, which equals $A^T-A$ only if $A^T=A$. In general it is skew-symmetric, not symmetric.
Example: $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ gives $A^T-A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, which is not symmetric.

qs.q: If $A$, $B$ and $C$ are three matrices such that $C=AB$, then $C^T=$ ----
e: The transpose of a product reverses the order: $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$.
Size check: if $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $B^T$ is $p\times n$ and $A^T$ is $n\times m$, so $B^TA^T$ is $p\times m$, the size of $C^T$.
$A^TB^T$ is generally not even defined, and $A^T+B^T$ has no relation to a product.
